newsitem.title: GERMANY: Southern nations could endanger euro - German banker.
newsitem.headline: Southern nations could endanger euro - German banker.

text.p: The stability of Europe's common currency, the Euro, hinges on southern European nations being excluded from the first group of nations to join the currency union in 1999, a top German banker said on Thursday.

"Union must begin with Germany, France, the Benelux nations, Ireland and Austria, but not immediately with the Mediterranean nations," Ulrich Cartellieri, board member at Germany's largest commercial bank Deutsche Bank AG, said.
The text of Cartellieri's speech, delivered in Luxembourg, was made available in Frankfurt.
The comments add weight to a growing perception that Germany is not interested in having the so-called "Club Med" nations enter the currency union at its launch in 1999.
At the same time German policy makers have generally said they expected southern European nations would be ready to join the union at a later date, but before 2002.
Echoing other policy makers' comments, Cartellieri warned that "it would be dangerous if nations joined (the union) by managing to meet the EMU criteria through a one-off effort."
The risks associated with letting nations join who only fulfilled the inflation criterion for the first time in 1997 must not be overlooked, Cartellieri said.
Nations' 1997 economic data will be used to determine which countries will be allowed to join the union, scheduled to begin on January 1, 1999.
Although it would be regretable if Britain did not join the union at the beginning, Cartellieri said its absence would allow the core nations to speed up European integration.
"We need to push on with the economic and political integration in Europe in the knowledge that the U.K. will join a successful currency union rather sooner than later,' he said.

London will play a key role for financial markets whether it is a member of the currency union or not, Cartellieri said. He added it was an illusion continental financial centres would benefit if Britain did not participate in the currency union.
Separately Cartellieri urged that France should declare, even before joining EMU, that it will stick to a realistic currency relationship with the mark.

France would not benefit from a devaluation against the mark but rather would profit from "a declaration of the will to stick to a currency relationship (with the mark) that has proven to be realistic for years," Cartellieri said.
"Such a declaration, supported by the firm political will of the government and the central bank, could secure the process towards the currency union," he added.
